summary: Extends TWAMP, the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, to let the control and test protocols use different security modes at the same time. It also creates an IANA registry for further TWAMP features.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5618 adds an option to TWAMP, the protocol that measures network performance by sending test packets and timing the replies. It lets the connection that sets the measurement up be protected with the stronger method, while the test packets themselves are sent without protection. The RFC also sets up a registry of the security modes TWAMP can use, so that more can be added later.

subtitle: Lets the control part of a TWAMP measurement be protected while the test packets themselves travel unencrypted.

tldr.problem: In TWAMP the control connection and the measurement packets normally share one security mode. That forces a choice: protect the control messages strongly and pay for it on every test packet too, or leave both weak. The control connection carries few packets, so it can afford stronger protection than the test stream can.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a fourth value to the 32-bit Modes field, value 8, which sets a new bit meaning that the test protocol runs unauthenticated while the control protocol keeps its stronger protection. A server advertises the modes it supports in its greeting, the client asks for the mixed mode, and the sender and reflector then use unauthenticated test packets.
tldr.outcome: The result is a way to protect the control connection strongly without slowing the measurement down with per-packet cryptography. The RFC also asks IANA for a registry of TWAMP modes, so that further modes can be added one bit at a time.

facts.label: First 28 bits
facts.value: Must be zero when no other features are activated

today: RFC 5618 is a Proposed Standard from August 2009. It updates RFC 5357, the TWAMP specification, by adding a fourth mode value and asking IANA for a registry of TWAMP modes. The security modes it builds on are those of the OWAMP control protocol in RFC 4656.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, TWAMP, is an extension of the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol, OWAMP. The TWAMP specification gathered wide review as it approached completion, and the by-products were several recommendations for new features in TWAMP. There is a growing number of TWAMP implementations, and widespread usage is expected.

This memo describes a simple extension for TWAMP: the option to use different security modes in the TWAMP-Control and TWAMP-Test protocols, which the RFC calls the mixed security mode. It also describes a new IANA registry for additional features, called the TWAMP Modes registry.

When the Server and the Control-Client have agreed to use the mixed security mode during control connection setup, then the Control-Client, the Server, the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector must all conform to the requirements of this mode. The memo updates the TWAMP specification itself.
sections.plainLanguage: TWAMP measures a path by sending packets and timing the answers. This RFC lets the part that sets the measurement up be secured more strongly than the packets being measured, because there are far fewer of the former.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The purpose of the memo is to describe and specify an extension for TWAMP, and to request the establishment of a registry for future TWAMP extensions.

The scope is limited to one thing: the extension of the modes of operation through the assignment of one new value in the Modes field, while retaining backward compatibility with existing TWAMP implementations. The new value adds the optional ability to use different security modes in the TWAMP-Control and TWAMP-Test protocols. The motivation is to permit the low-packet-rate TWAMP-Control protocol to use a stronger mode of integrity protection than the one used in the TWAMP-Test protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is deliberately small: one more value in a bit field that already existed, so old and new implementations can still talk to each other. The point of the new value is to let the rarely used control connection be protected more strongly than the stream of test packets.

sections.title: Extended Control Connection Setup
sections.content:
The TWAMP-Control protocol is a derivative of the OWAMP-Control protocol and coordinates a two-way measurement capability. All TWAMP-Control messages are similar in format and follow the guidelines of the OWAMP-Control specification, with the exceptions described in the TWAMP specification and in this section. All OWAMP-Control messages apply to TWAMP-Control except for the Fetch-Session command.

TWAMP-Control connection establishment follows the same procedure as before. This extended mode assigns one new bit position, and value, which allows the test protocol to operate in unauthenticated mode while the control protocol operates in encrypted mode. The complete set of TWAMP Mode values is then 0 for reserved, 1 for unauthenticated, 2 for authenticated, 4 for encrypted, and 8 for the new mixed mode in which the test protocol is unauthenticated and the control protocol is encrypted.

In the original OWAMP and TWAMP Modes field, setting bit position 0, 1 or 2 indicated the security mode of the control protocol, and the test protocol inherited the same mode. In this extension, when the Control-Client sets Modes Field bit position 3, it stops that inheritance, and each protocol's mode is as specified. When the desired TWAMP-Test protocol mode is identical to the control session mode, the corresponding Modes Field bit, position 0, 1 or 2, is set by the Control-Client. The control and test protocols use the mode in each column corresponding to the bit position set in the Modes Field.

The security measures of the TWAMP-Control protocol are identical in the authenticated and encrypted modes, so only one new bit position is needed to convey the single mixed security mode.

The value of the Modes Field sent by the Server in the Server-Greeting message is the bit-wise OR of the modes, that is the bit positions, that it is willing to support during the session. The last four bits of the 32-bit Modes Field are therefore used. When no other features are activated, the first 28 bits must be zero. A client conforming to this extension may ignore the values in the first 28 bits, or it may support other features that are communicated in those bit positions.
sections.plainLanguage: The mode is chosen with bits in a 32-bit field. The three old bits say how the control connection is protected, and the test packets used to inherit that choice. A fourth bit says the test packets are not protected, so the control connection can stay strong.

sections.title: Extended TWAMP Test
sections.content:
The TWAMP-Test protocol is similar to the OWAMP-Test protocol, with the exception that the Session-Reflector transmits test packets to the Session-Sender in response to each test packet it receives. TWAMP defines two different test packet formats, one for packets transmitted by the Session-Sender and one for packets transmitted by the Session-Reflector. As with the OWAMP-Test protocol, there are three security modes, unauthenticated, authenticated and encrypted, and these also determine the test packet format.

This extension makes it possible to use the TWAMP-Test unauthenticated mode regardless of the mode used in the TWAMP-Control protocol. When the Server has identified the ability to support the mixed security mode, the Control-Client has selected the mixed security mode in its Set-Up-Response, and the Server has responded with a zero Accept field in the Server-Start message, these extensions are required.

On the sending side, the Session-Sender must follow the same procedure and guidelines for the packet format and content as before, with two exceptions: the send schedule is not used, and the Session-Sender must support the mixed security mode. On the reflecting side, the Session-Reflector must follow the procedures of the TWAMP specification with the extension that it must support the mixed security mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The test packet format follows from the security mode, so saying the test packets are unauthenticated also says what those packets look like. Both the sender and the reflector have to support the new mode once the control connection has asked for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extended mixed mode of operation permits stronger security and integrity protection on the TWAMP-Control protocol while simultaneously emphasising accuracy or efficiency on the TWAMP-Test protocol. It therefore makes it possible to increase overall security when compared with the previous options, in the case where resource constraints would have forced less security for TWAMP-Control and the conditions are such that the use of unauthenticated TWAMP-Test is not a significant concern.

The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant here as well, and the RFC points to the OWAMP and TWAMP specifications for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The trade is deliberate: the measurement traffic is left unprotected, and the control traffic, which is what an attacker would use to change what is being measured, is protected as well as it can be.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo adds one security mode bit position and value beyond those in the OWAMP-Control specification and describes the behaviour when the new mode is used. IANA created a registry for the TWAMP Modes field, which is a recognised extension mechanism for TWAMP.

Modes are specified in the TWAMP Server Greeting messages and Set-up Response messages, and are currently indicated by setting single bits in the 32-bit Modes Field. More complex encoding may be used in the future, so the registry can contain a total of 2^32 possible assignments. Because the registry can hold that many values, and because TWAMP is an IETF protocol, it must be updated only by IETF Review. New features are expected to be assigned using monotonically increasing single bit positions in the range 0 to 31, unless there is a good reason to do otherwise.

No experimental values are currently assigned for the Modes Registry. The initial contents are the same list as the mode values: 0 reserved, 1 unauthenticated, 2 authenticated, 4 encrypted, and 8 for the unauthenticated test protocol with the encrypted control protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The modes get a registry of their own so that more can be added over time. Each new mode takes the next free bit, and the first 28 bits of the field are left for other features.

items.label: Unauthenticated
items.desc: The security mode of the control protocol, inherited by the test protocol.

items.label: Authenticated
items.desc: The security mode of the control protocol, inherited by the test protocol.

items.label: Encrypted
items.desc: The security mode of the control protocol, inherited by the test protocol.

items.label: Unauth. TEST protocol, Encrypted CONTROL
items.desc: The new mixed security mode, set with bit position 3, in which the test packets are sent without protection while the control protocol keeps its stronger one.

cells: The same as the control protocol

viz.caption: WHO HAS TO IMPLEMENT THE MIXED MODE

items.title: Control-Client
items.text: Asks for the mixed security mode in its Set-Up-Response, and stops the test protocol from inheriting the control mode.

items.title: Server
items.text: Advertises the mixed mode in its Server-Greeting, and answers with a zero Accept field in the Server-Start message.

items.title: Session-Sender
items.text: Must support the mixed mode, and sends its test packets without the send schedule and without protection.

items.title: Session-Reflector
items.text: Must support the mixed mode, and sends the reply packets in the matching format.
